reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Leah turned three today. There was a party in the backyard. Balloons sat near the fence. Grandpa set a cake on the table.

Leah wanted to blow out the candle. She took a big breath. She blew. The flame stayed on. She blew again. The flame still stayed on.

"Try once more," said Mama. Leah stood near the cake. She blew slow and long. The candle went out. Everyone clapped.

"One big breath," Leah said. "One big breath makes it go out."

Then she hopped on one foot. She hopped again. The candle was out because of her big breath. The party went on. Leah ate cake with her friends.

"Happy birthday, Leah," said Grandpa.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Beatrice went to the store with Dad. She wanted milk. But the milk was gone from the little shelf. "Where is the milk?" she asked. Dad said, "Maybe a big box in the back."

They walked to the back. Beatrice saw a big door. It was the cold room. Dad opened it. Cold air came out fast. Beatrice shivered. Brrr! She saw little milk jugs and big milk jugs. The big ones were up high. The little ones were down low.

Beatrice took a little jug. It was very cold. She held it with two hands. Then they passed the bakery. The bread there was hot. "The cold room made the milk cold," Beatrice said. "This hot oven makes the bread hot!" Dad smiled. "That is the answer," he said. "You found it all by yourself." Beatrice laughed. "Cold and hot are opposites. But my tummy likes them both!" At home, Dad poured warm milk in her cup. Beatrice took a big sip.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Sofia wanted to play the guessing game. But she did not know the rules yet. "What if I get it wrong?" she asked. Mama sat close and held her hand. "We learn it together," said Mama.

Mama held up a lemon. "Close your eyes. Now smell." Sofia sniffed with her nose. "It smells sour!" she said. "Your nose knows," said Mama. Next came a bell. It rang, and Sofia heard it fast with her ears. Then Mama let her touch a soft blanket. "My hands feel it!" said Sofia. Mama gave her a sweet berry. Sofia tasted it with her tongue. At last Sofia opened her eyes and looked at the moon in the window. "My eyes see the moon!" she said.

"Now it is your turn," said Mama. "Show me all five." Sofia pointed to her eyes, her ears, her nose, her tongue, and her hands. "Five!" she counted. Mama clapped. Sofia turned around and around, laughing. Then she sat on Mama's lap, warm and safe, and looked at the moon one more time. "Good night, moon," said Sofia.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Grayson ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. His teacher had put a new sign on the wall. "Today the sign says sunny," said Grayson. He clapped his hands. Now he could dress the big teddy bear for outside.

But which clothes? Grayson picked snow boots and a thick coat. "Too hot," said his friend Mia. She pointed at the window. The sun was bright. The sky was all blue and warm. Grayson touched the coat. It was heavy and hot in his hand. Then he got it. Snowy days need warm coats. Sunny days do not.

So Grayson found a little sun hat and cool shorts. He glued a paper sun onto the bear's shirt. "Perfect," said Mia. Outside, the sun felt warm on Grayson's arms.

A shy girl named Ruby peeked at the bear. "Can I hold it?" she asked. Grayson smiled big. "Yes! The bear loves the sun." Then they ran together into the bright, warm yard.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread. She reached far across the table. Her elbow bumped her cup. Milk spilled onto Dad's hat, the one he had set on his chair.

"Sorry, Dad," said Wren. Dad got a towel and wiped the hat. "That's okay," he said.

Wren tried again. "Bread," she said. Dad just looked at her. Then Mom smiled. "Try the nice word," Mom said. Wren said, "Bread, please." Dad passed the bread right away. The word worked!

Wren took a bite. Then she pushed her chair back and slid down. "My feet are stuck," she said. "Can you help me, please?" Dad helped her sit up tall.

"Thank you, Dad," said Wren. Dad kissed her head. Wren ate the bread. The lazy cat slept under her chair and did not help at all.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Livia could not find Bunny. Bunny was her best toy. "Where are you?" she called.

She peeked under the bed. No Bunny. She peeked in the toy box. No Bunny. "Think, Livia," she said. "Where did I go today?"

Livia had played outside. She had played with paint. She had eaten a snack. She put her hands on her cheeks. "I will go back to each place," she said. "Toys do not walk. Bunny stays where I put Bunny down."

First she went outside. Bunny was not far, by the big tree. No Bunny there. Then she came back in. She peeked at the paint table. No Bunny. But she saw something. A small pink color on the floor. It was a paint dot. It made a little line.

Livia followed the paint dots. Dot, dot, dot. They went past the chair. They went by the sofa. They stopped at the laundry basket. Livia peeked inside. There was Bunny! Bunny had paint on one ear. Bunny had been washing!

"Mom!" Livia called. "I found Bunny!" Mom came fast and smiled. "Bunny has paint on his ear," said Mom. "Let's wash him nice and clean." Livia washed Bunny's ear with a soft cloth.

Then Livia hugged Bunny tight. "No more painting with you," she whispered. Bunny's ear was clean and soft again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna counted on her fingers. "Seven days," she said. "Seven sleeps, Grandma!"

Sienna wanted to paint a picture with Grandma on the very first morning. But Grandma sat on the couch. Her eyes were droopy. "Not yet, little one," Grandma said.

Sienna looked at the big clock on the wall. It was morning, but Grandma was sleepy. "Why are you sleepy, Grandma?" she asked. "You slept last night."

Grandma smiled. "My home is far away. I sat on a train for many hours. Long rides make me tired."

Sienna thought about that. The train ride made Grandma tired. That was why. So Grandma needed more sleep first.

Sienna got a soft blanket. She tucked it around Grandma. "Sleep now," she whispered. "Paint later." Grandma closed her eyes.

The clock ticked and ticked. At lunch time, Grandma woke up. "I feel much better now," she said.

They sat at the kitchen table. Sienna painted a red apple. Grandma painted a yellow sun. The paint smelled like rain and flowers.

"See, Grandma," said Sienna. "You slept, and now you are not tired anymore."

Grandma laughed and kissed her head. "You are my smart helper."

There were still six sleeps left. "Tomorrow," said Sienna, "we paint a big blue cat."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Emilia wanted toast with butter. Mama gave her a small knife. The butter was cold and hard. Emilia pushed it on the toast. The toast tore. A little hole showed.

"Try the soft butter," said Mama. The soft butter sat in a small dish by the warm toaster. Emilia dipped her knife. She spread it slow. The butter went on smooth. "Soft butter does not tear the toast," said Emilia.

Next came the milk. Emilia held the jug up high. Milk splashed on the table. A tiny ant came to look at the little puddle. "Hello, ant," said Emilia. She did not talk to it for long. She had work to do.

She set the cup on the table. She poured slow and low, close to the cup. The milk went in. Not one drop fell. She poured the last bit. The cup was full.

Emilia sat down. She bit her smooth, buttery toast. She drank her milk. The ant waved its legs and crawled away.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Anthony rides the big city bus. He holds his bunny in his lap. Then the bus bumps. Anthony holds on to the seat. Where did bunny go?

Anthony looks down. He looks under the seat. No bunny. He looks by his feet. No bunny. Then he thinks, "The bus went bump. Maybe bunny fell." He bends down low. He peeks under the seat again, way in the back. There is bunny! It is a soft little nest under the seat, and bunny sits in it.

Anthony pulls bunny out. "The bus went bump, so you fell," he says. "That is true." He hugs bunny tight. A kind lady smiles at him. "Your bunny is dirty," she says. Anthony wipes bunny's face with his sleeve. Now bunny is clean. The bus stops, and Anthony waves to the lady. "Bye bye! We found our nest!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist. "First time," said Mama. Florence looked out the window. She saw a fish shop go by. Big fish, little fish, all on ice.

The bus stopped and stopped. "Are we near?" asked Florence. "Not yet," said Mama. "We wait." Florence waited. She counted the buttons on her coat. One, two, three.

At last the bus stopped near a little office. A man in a blue shirt smiled. "Hello, Florence. I am the dentist." He had a small mirror on a stick. "Open your mouth big and wide," he said. "Then I can see your back teeth."

Florence closed her mouth. Then she opened it a little. Then she opened it very wide. The dentist looked and looked. "I can see all your teeth now," he said. "Let's count them." He counted one by one. Then he put some tooth paste on a little brush. It tickled. It tasted like strawberries.

Florence sat up. "My teeth are clean," she said. The dentist gave her a sticker with a fish on it. Florence put it near her heart. "Open wide again," she said, "so you can see my sticker."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Leah ran to the swings. But a line of kids stood there. Four kids, then five kids. Leah got in the line too.

"I want to swing now," she said.

"Wait for your turn," said a big boy. "Let's count."

He clapped his hands. "One, two, three." The kids sang with him. "Four, five, six." Leah sang too. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!"

The first boy hopped off his swing. Then a girl. One kid went each time they counted to ten.

Leah watched and watched. At last she was at the front. One, two, three, four, five. Her turn came fast!

She swung up high. Her hands held the clean, cold chain. She laughed.

Then she saw a small boy behind her, waiting in the line. He looked sad.

Leah counted with him. "One, two, three." She swung and counted. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

She jumped off. "Your turn now," she said.

The boy smiled a big, happy smile. "One, two, three!" he sang, pumping his legs.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Arthur ran to Grandpa's garden. "I want big carrots!" he said. Grandpa gave him tiny seeds. Arthur made a little hole in the middle of the dirt. He dropped three seeds in. Then he covered them up.

Every day Arthur looked. Nothing grew. Arthur forgot to give the seeds water! Grandpa filled a small can. Arthur poured water on the dirt. "Drink, seeds, drink!" he said.

The next morning was very cold. The water in the can went freeze, hard as ice! But the dirt was soft. Two little green leaves popped up. Arthur jumped up and down. "The water made them grow!" he said.

Grandpa smiled. Soon the leaves grew tall. Under the dirt, a yellow carrot got fat. Arthur pulled it out. "My carrot! I grew it!"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming to stay! She would sleep in Juliette's room for seven whole days. Juliette counted on her fingers. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven! "Grandma needs a bed," said Mama. "Can you help make it?" Yes! Juliette could help!

They went to the big market to get things. Juliette waved at the apple man. She waved at the bread lady. Everyone knew Grandma was coming! "Grandma likes tea," said Mama. "But her tea mug stayed at her own house." Oh no. Grandma would have no mug for seven whole days!

Juliette looked and looked. A red mug. A green mug. Then she saw it. A tiny blue mug with a duck on it. "This one!" she said. It was little, just like Grandma's hands. It fit right inside her own fingers. She held it up high. "Grandma's mug!"

At home, Juliette made the bed. She put a soft blanket on it. She put the duck mug by the lamp. Grandma's hat sat on the chair, waiting too. Then the door opened. Grandma was here! She picked up the little mug. "A duck for my tea!" said Grandma. "I am sorry I left my mug home. But this one is better." Juliette clapped and clapped. Seven days of tea with Grandma! Juliette poured the very first cup.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Owen ran to the park with his red ball. He felt so excited. His tummy felt like bouncing.

Then a big dog ran up. The dog barked very loud. Owen felt scared. He hid behind a tree. His hands shook. Why was the dog barking? Owen peeked out. The dog was looking at his ball, not at him. Maybe the dog was angry because the ball went into her yard! Owen threw the ball far. The dog ran and got it. Then the dog wagged her tail. She was happy now. Owen laughed. "The dog was loud because she wanted my ball," he said.

A girl came by. Her name was Mia. She was crying. Her ice cream had fallen. Drip, drip, on the ground. Now it was smelly too, because a goose came to bite it. Owen gave Mia his ball to hold. She stopped crying. She smiled. Owen felt warm inside. "Want to play?" said Mia. Owen threw the ball high, and they both ran after it.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Penelope walked into her classroom. The sun sat low in the window. Yesterday she found a red leaf at the park. It was big and shiny. She wanted to show it to her friend Sam today. She looked in her bag. The leaf was not there. The leaf was still at home, on top of her table.

"Where is your leaf?" asked Sam. "It is at home," said Penelope. "I found it yesterday. But yesterday is all done. I cannot go back and get it now." Her tummy felt a little tight. Then she had an idea. "Tomorrow I will bring it," she said. "Tomorrow is the day after today. First we sleep, then it comes."

All day they painted pictures. Later, the teacher rang the bell. "The day went fast," said Penelope. She walked to the door with Sam. "Tonight I will put the leaf in my bag," she said. "Then tomorrow it will be here." Sam smiled. "I will wait for it," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Jasmine had a library book about rainbows. She wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime she hugged the book tight.

"Can this book stay with me always?" she asked.

Mom shook her head. "The library book must go back on Friday. Other kids will read it too."

Jasmine pouted. Then she had an idea. "Can I draw my own rainbow book?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "That one is yours to keep."

Jasmine took paper and crayons. She drew a big rainbow. She drew a small rainbow. She asked Mom to write the words. Mom wrote "Rainbow" on the first page. Jasmine pointed at the letters.

"Those are real words?" she asked.

"They are true words," said Mom. "Books start at the front. We read this way."

Jasmine turned the pages one by one, front to back. Then she put her book under her pillow.

"Friday can come now," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Henry sat at the little red table. He wanted to paint a big orange pumpkin. But there was no orange paint.

His teacher pointed to the cups. "Red, yellow, blue," she said. Henry said them too. "Red, yellow, blue." He touched each cup. "One, two, three."

He looked at the red cup. He looked at the yellow cup. He put his brush in the red. Dab. Then he put it in the yellow. Dab. He stirred on the white paper. The paint turned orange!

Henry laughed. "Red and yellow make orange!" he said.

His friend Mia looked sad. She wanted green for her frog. Henry showed her the blue cup. Then the yellow cup. "Blue and yellow make green," he said.

Mia dabbed blue. Then yellow. Green! Her frog got a big green back.

The brush tickled Henry's fingers with paint. He made a small orange pillow for his pumpkin to sit on. Mia made a green lily pad.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Henry. "Mix, mix, mix!"

"More pumpkins!" said Mia. Henry dipped his brush in the red again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Max ran to the red truck. Ben grabbed it too. "My turn!" said Max. He pulled. Ben pulled. The truck fell on the floor. A wheel came off.

Max picked up the wheel. He tried to put it back on. It would not go on. Teacher Mia sat with them. She held up her hand. "Let's count to twenty," she said. "Ben goes first. Then Max."

Ben drove the truck around the rug. Max counted. He counted to twenty twice. Then Ben put the truck in Max's hands. Max drove it fast, past the blocks and past the pillow corner.

A small spider came out from under the truck. "It's tickly!" said Max. "My sock feels itchy." He laughed and wiggled his foot. "Ben, look!" he said. "Trucks carry spiders!"

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Camille put on her warm blanket cape. She ran to the ice rink with Dad. The ice was all white and shiny. Kids were playing on the soft mats by the boards.

Dad put a hoop on the floor. "Try to throw the beanbag in!" Camille threw it high. It went way over the hoop. She threw it fast. It went far away. "Why does it keep missing?" she asked. She looked at the hoop. It was close. She tried one more time, soft and slow. The beanbag went up and sank right into the hoop. "It was too hard!" she said. "Soft works!" Dad clapped.

Then Dad rolled her a big red ball. Camille held out one hand. The ball hit her fingers and bounced off. She held out both hands. The big ball landed right in them. "Two hands catch the big ball!" she said. Dad threw it again. She caught it again. The zamboni drove past on the ice. "Look, pretty lights!" she said. "Throw it high, Dad!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Quinn stood at the pet store. She held a little box with holes. Inside was her new bunny, Pip.

"Is Pip sad in the box?" Quinn asked. "He is not sad," said Dad. "He is shy. New homes feel big to bunnies."

At home, Quinn put the box on the floor. She opened the lid. Pip did not hop out. He just sat still. Quinn waited. Then she put a small carrot near the door. Pip sniffed it. His nose went wiggle, wiggle. Then he hopped out!

"He came out because of the carrot," Quinn said. "Smells help him feel safe." Dad smiled. "Yes. Bunnies follow their noses."

Pip hopped to his water bowl. He drank a little sip. Quinn sat very still on the floor. "I will not grab you," she said softly. Pip hopped close to her shoe. His ears touched her sock.

Quinn reached out one gentle hand. Pip sniffed her fingers. Then he settled down in a soft warm ball. Dad put a blanket by the bowl. "This is his spot," Dad said.

Quinn watched her bunny sleep. "Good night, Pip," she said. "This is your home now."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels.

"I am hungry," said Felix. Mom reached back her hand. In the bag were a banana, a small toy duck, and some crackers. Felix picked up the duck. He put it near his mouth. Then he shook his head. "No," said Felix. "Ducks are toys. Toys do not go in my tummy."

"Smart boy," said Mom. Felix counted what he could eat. "One, banana. Two, crackers. Banana is food. Crackers are food." He peeled the banana. It smelled sweet. He took a big bite.

Outside the window, Felix saw cows. "One cow, two cows, three cows!" he said. "Cows are animals." Then Felix saw something in the road. "Stop, Mom! Dog!" Mom stopped the car. The dog ran safely across. Felix waved his banana at the window. "Bye, dog! I leave some crackers for you!" Mom put two crackers on the grass by the fence.

The car went on. The wheels went bump, bump. Felix found a surprise in his pocket. It was a little toy car! "A toy!" he said. "Not food. Just for playing." He made the toy car zoom on his knee. Then he ate his crackers, one crunch at a time.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story: Alice ran to the big slide. But her friend Sam was there first. Sam stood at the top and would not come down. "We can count and take turns," said Alice. "How does counting help?" asked Sam. "We count to ten, then we swap." Alice began. "One, two, three." Sam listened from the top. "Four, five, six." Alice kept going, slow and steady. "Seven, eight, nine." Sam slid down with a little bump in the sand. "Ten!" said Alice. Now it was her turn. She climbed up and slid down fast. The slide felt cool, not slimy like the pond rocks at home. They counted to ten again and again, back and forth, all morning. "Counting is like a dream," said Sam happily. Alice laughed and began again: "One, two, three."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Hayden went to the library with his mom. It was cloudy outside. Inside, the lights felt warm.

Hayden wanted the big red book about a cat. It was on a high shelf. He reached and reached. He could not get it.

"Help, please," he said to the librarian. She smiled. "Of course," she said. She got the cat book down.

Hayden hugged the book. "Thank you," he said.

He sat at the little table. One book, two books, three books. He counted his stack. Then his elbow bumped a cup. The cup tipped over. Water ran across the table.

"Sorry," Hayden said to the librarian. "It fell because my elbow hit it," he said.

She helped him cover the wet spot with a towel. Then she handed him something small. It was a cat sticker.

"For me?" asked Hayden.

The librarian nodded. "For saying please and thank you and sorry."

Hayden put the sticker on his shirt. It was a tiny orange cat. He grinned all the way home.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Brooks had a cough. It kept him awake at night. Mom said, "We will go to the pharmacy."

At the pharmacy, Brooks sat in the cart. He saw tall shelves. He saw boxes and bottles. Mom found the honey. She showed the jar to Brooks. "Honey can help your throat," she said.

At home, Mom gave Brooks a small spoon of honey. It was sweet and slow in his mouth. He swallowed it. The scratchy feeling got quiet. That night, Brooks coughed less. He slept in his warm bed. In the morning he said, "Mom, the honey made my cough stop." Mom smiled and put the jar back on the shelf. "One more spoon for breakfast," she said. Brooks ran to the kitchen table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Louis stood at the little table in cooking class. Today he would make toast and pour milk. His heart went bump, bump. He wanted to do it all by himself.

First the toast. Louis pushed the butter with his knife. The butter would not spread. It tore a hole in the toast. "Try small bits of soft butter," said Miss Ana. Louis took a tiny bit and rubbed it on. It went on smooth. "Small bits work," said Louis.

Next the milk. Louis held the jug far above the cup. Milk splashed out. It ran onto the table. A drop began to chase his friend Mia's plate. Louis moved the jug down low, close to the cup. He tipped it slow. The milk went in. Not one drop fell.

"Look, Miss Ana," said Louis. He lifted his cup up high. "I did it, all by myself!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Connor was in his playroom. His hands were dirty from the sand table. He wanted his big red truck to zoom fast down the ramp. It went slow. Too slow. Connor let go again. Slow, slow, slow. He began to wonder why.

Then he tried his small blue car. It went fast. Very, very fast. It zoomed right past the truck. The big truck was heavy. The small car was light. "That is why!" said Connor. "Big goes slow. Small goes fast."

Next to the ramp was his toy kettle. It had warm water inside. Connor touched it. Hot. He dipped his dirty truck in cold water from his cup. The cup felt cold. "Hot cup, cold cup," he said. He washed the truck until it was clean.

Connor held the car up high. "Want to zoom again?" he asked. The little car zoomed down the ramp and bumped right into the big, clean truck.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Asher ran to the park with Mama. He wanted to play on the slide. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Asher held her hand.

Near the slide, there was a big grill. Smoke came up from it. Asher pointed. "Hot," said Mama. She held her hand near, not on it. Asher put his hand near too. He felt the warm air. He pulled his hand back. "The grill is hot because of the fire," he said. "I will not touch it."

Asher slid down the slide. Then he slid down again. He got thirsty. Mama said, "Let us bring your cup." Asher drank his juice. It was cold. "Cold juice, hot grill," he said. Mama laughed.

Then a little dog came by. It had Asher's red ball in its mouth! "Woof," said the dog. It dropped the ball at Asher's feet. Asher was happy. "Thank you, dog," he said. He threw the ball, and the dog ran after it.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story: Isaiah sat in his big car seat. He held a small cup of ice. Mom said, "Hold it tight. We will drive fast now." The sun came in the window. It was hot on his hands. Isaiah looked down. His ice was getting small and wet. Drip, drip, on his pants. "Mom, why is my ice melting?" he asked. "Because the sun is hot," Mom said. "Ice melts in hot places." Isaiah thought hard. He saw the little window by the vent. Cold air blew out of it. He moved his cup to the cold spot. He held it there. Soon the ice stopped dripping. It stayed big and cold. "The cold air wins!" Isaiah said. Mom smiled. Then Dad said, "Uh oh. Now we drive slow. Red light." The car stopped. Isaiah giggled and licked his ice. "Slow is good," he said. "Slow helps me eat it all."

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Raphael went to the dentist. He wanted a sticker at the end. The friendly dentist said, "Open wide!" Raphael opened his mouth. Then it was time for a snack. Raphael ran to the table and grabbed an apple.

The dentist said, "Wait! Wash your hands first." Raphael put his hands under the water. "Too fast," said the dentist. "Use soap. Wash for twenty seconds. Sing happy birthday two times." Raphael rubbed the soap on his palms. He sang the song. In the middle of the song, he saw bubbles cover his hands. When the song ended, the bubbles were gone. His hands were clean and shiny.

Raphael ate his apple. "The soap got the germs off," he said. "That is why I wash!" He did not skip the sink after the toilet either. The dentist gave him a big sticker. "Two hands clean," said Raphael, holding it up.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Eva climbed the school bus. She held the rail with both hands. Her mommy had pinned a pink tag on her coat. The tag had her name on it. "I can write my name," Eva said. "But Mommy wrote it for me."

She sat by the window. The bus was big and yellow. One driver. Two big mirrors. Three rows of seats. Eva looked out. She saw a red nose on a clown poster. She saw trees going by, one, two, three.

The bus stopped. Eva looked at her pink tag. Then she looked out the window. There was a sign. It said her school's name, just like her tag said her name. The bus stops at the school with my name on it, she thought. A teacher with a smile came up the steps. She looked at Eva's tag. "Hello, Eva," the teacher said.

The door opened with a whoosh. Eva took the teacher's hand. One step. Two steps. Three steps down. On the ground lay a small pink flower. It had fallen out of a girl's basket. Eva picked it up and put it in her pocket. Then she walked through the big door.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Arlo wants to make a paper garden. He cuts out one sun, two clouds, and three red flowers.

He puts a flower on the paper. He tips the paper up. The flower slides off. "Guess it wants to fall," he says. Why does it fall?

Mama hands him a glue stick. Arlo rubs it on the back of a flower. The glue feels cool and slippery. He presses the flower down. He counts, "One flower, two flowers, three flowers." He tips the paper again. The flowers stay!

"So the glue was wet," Arlo says. "Now it is dry. Dry glue holds the flowers."

He adds the sun and the clouds. He tips the paper way up high. Nothing falls. "My garden stays," he says. "One sun, two clouds, three flowers. All stuck!"

Arlo runs to the window. "Look, Mama! My garden is on the wall!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Avery sat at the paint table. Her class had a goldfish. It was the class pet. The fish swam in slow circles. "Hello, fish," said Avery.

Avery wanted to paint the fish. She had yellow paint. She had blue paint too. But the fish was green.

She painted with yellow. The fish looked wrong. Then a drip fell. Blue paint spilled into the yellow. The colors moved together. The puddle turned green.

Avery looked and looked. "Blue and yellow make green," she said. She dabbed her brush in the new green. She painted the fish carefully, slow and small.

The teacher leaned down. "That looks just like him," she said.

Avery held up her paper next to the bowl. Green fish, green paint. The fish blew a tiny bubble.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her mama gave her a hug. Then her mama waved and went down the hall.

Elizabeth held her new backpack. She looked around the room. There were little red hooks on the wall. Each hook had a name on it. She saw a hook with "Elizabeth" on it. She hung her backpack on that hook. She hung her coat there too.

At play time, Elizabeth made a picture. She used the glue bottle. A drop of glue got on her fingers. "Oooh, it feels slimy," she said. She rubbed her fingers together. The glue got sticky and stringy.

Her teacher brought a wet cloth. "This will help," she said. Elizabeth wiped her hands. The sticky glue came off. "The water took the glue away," Elizabeth said. "Thank you," she said to her teacher.

When it was time to go home, Elizabeth looked at the wall. She found the hook with her name. Her coat was right there. "The name tells me where my things go," she said. She pulled up her zipper all by herself. Then she ran to the door to find her mama.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Beau sat in his big car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. It was windy outside. The trees waved their leaves. Beau's tummy made a growl. "I want a snack!" he said.

Mom said, "Look in your bag." Beau dug in the bag. He pulled out a toy car. Vroom! But a toy car is not a snack. He pulled out his teddy bear. He hugged the teddy. But a teddy is not a snack either. Then he found his book. He looked at the picture of a duck. But a book is not a snack! Beau dug deeper. His hand found something yellow. It was a banana! A banana is a food. Beau peeled it all by himself. He took a big bite. Yum! His tummy went quiet.

The car stopped at a red light. Beau had to wait. He waved his banana at Mom. Mom smiled and said, "One more bite, and then we are home." Beau took the biggest bite of all.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Myles took her to the park. It was spring, and the flowers were out.

"Look at the ducks," said Myles. "Look, look, look!" Grandma looked and laughed. They ran to the swings. They ran to the slide. They ran to the big tree.

Then Grandma sat down on a bench. Her eyes went closed. Myles pulled her hand. "Swing more!" But Grandma did not move. She was asleep. Grandmas get tired when they run, because their legs are old and slow. Myles saw this all by himself.

"Grandma needs a rest," he said. He sat by her feet. A duck came near. "Shh," said Myles. "Grandma needs a rest."

Soon Grandma opened her eyes. "Did I miss the ducks?" she asked. "You missed three ducks," said Myles. Grandma laughed and laughed. Then she stood up, took his hand, and said, "Show me all three."

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Nora was at Ben's house. Ben had a tablet. Nora wanted to draw on it. But the screen was dark. She tapped it. Nothing happened. Why was it dark?

"Try the little round button," said Ben. Nora pressed the round button at the side. Click. The screen lit up! It was bright and full of colors. "The button made it wake up," said Nora. She found the drawing app. It was the square with a paintbrush. She tapped it and drew a messy purple cat with six legs.

Then Mom called them for a snack. Nora put the tablet on the shelf, next to a big red book. "I press the button again later," she said.

After snack, she pressed the round button. Click. And there was her purple cat, still on the screen, waiting for her. "It remembers my cat," said Nora. She added one more leg.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Paisley saw a big blue bus at the park. It was a bookmobile! Books sat on little shelves inside. Paisley wanted a book about a red fire truck.

A lady in the bus smiled. "Would you like your own library card?" she asked. Paisley jumped up and down. "Yes! Yes! Yes!" she said.

The card felt rough on one side. Paisley held it tight. The lady found the fire truck book. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back next week so other kids can read it too."

Paisley stopped jumping. "I want to keep it forever," she said. Then she saw a boy at the shelf. He was looking for a truck book too. There were no more truck books. The boy looked sad. The boy was sad because the book was in Paisley's hands.

Paisley looked at her card. She looked at the boy. "You can read it after me," she said. "I will bring it back fast, fast, fast."

Paisley walked home with Mama. She hugged the book all the way. Every night they read about the red fire truck. The good feeling grew and grew.

On the last day, Paisley walked back to the bus. She gave the book to the boy. He sat down right away to read. "My turn next time!" said Paisley, waving her rough little card.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lennon went to the big cultural center with Mama and Nana. There was a party for Diwali. Music played. Little lamps glowed everywhere.

Lennon ran to the door. But a kind man stood there. He pointed down at his feet. He had no shoes on! "We take our shoes off here," said Mama. "That is why everyone is barefoot." Lennon looked down. Her shoes were on. That was wrong!

Mama helped her pull them off. Then Mama sent Lennon to put them in a shoe box by the wall. Lennon placed them in, so they would not get lost. Nana held her hand. They walked in together.

The floor was cool and smooth under Lennon's toes. She sat by the lamps. "Shoes off, then we go in," she said. Mama smiled and gave her a little lamp to hold.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Lucy ran to the park with Dad. The sun was warm on her face. "It is sunny today," she said. Dad spread a blanket on the grass. Lucy took off her shoes. The grass tickled her toes.

Then the wind came. It blew and blew. Lucy's hat flew off her head. "My hat!" she cried. The wind pushed it under a bush. Lucy ran to get it. Dirt was on the brim. Dad helped her brush it off. "The wind took my hat because it was loose," Lucy said. Dad nodded. "So we will tie it tight." He tied the strap under her chin. The wind blew again. The hat stayed on Lucy's head.

"Now I can keep my hat," Lucy said. She felt the warm sun again. A kind lady on the next blanket smiled at her. "Hold on tight," the lady said. Lucy laughed and held her hat with both hands.
